headline: High: shared filesystem and broad write/network privileges make prompt injection, data leakage, and cascading errors plausible by default.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Cursor can read/write workspace files and clipboard, and OpenHands can read/write files in its runtime; both also use MCP. A shared local filesystem or copied content can carry attacker-controlled instructions from one agent into the other, so injection is plausible even without a documented direct bridge.
conditions: IF the two agents exchange files through a shared workspace or mounted volume, prompt injection becomes actionable.
IF either agent treats file contents as trusted instructions, malicious content can steer tool use.
mitigations: Separate workspaces so no file is visible to both agents.
Disable copy/paste of untrusted agent output into the other agent.
Require a human review step before executing instructions found in files.
Use provenance labels on generated artifacts.
requires-engineering: add content-sanitization or instruction-stripping at the handoff boundary.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Cursor touches open files, workspace files, and clipboard contents; OpenHands touches files mounted into its runtime. If sensitive material is placed in a shared workspace or copied across, both agents can expose it through broad network egress and model-provider calls. The path exists in default-style coding workflows, though not every deployment shares data.
conditions: IF sensitive files are mounted into OpenHands and also opened in Cursor, both agents can process the same data class.
IF either agent sends file contents to a third-party model provider, leakage risk increases.
mitigations: Keep secrets out of shared workspaces.
Use separate per-agent repositories or mounts.
Disable clipboard transfer for sensitive sessions.
Route both agents to local-only models for sensitive tasks.
requires-engineering: enforce DLP or redaction before any outbound API call.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents have unrestricted filesystem write, shell execution, package installation, and git-state modification. Cursor shares state via the local filesystem, while OpenHands shares via mounted volume; concurrent edits to the same repo can overwrite each other or corrupt git state without locking, which is dangerous by default.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same repository or directory, write conflicts can occur.
IF either agent commits or rewrites git state without coordination, history corruption or lost work can occur.
mitigations: Assign each agent a separate checkout.
Serialize git writes with a lock file.
Pause one agent while the other applies patches.
Review diffs before any commit or rebase.
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level concurrency control.

D_cascading_error.rationale: Cursor runs an agent loop with multi-step tool use and OpenHands also executes shell/browser/editor actions inside a runtime sandbox. If OpenHands consumes Cursor-produced code or instructions as authoritative, mistakes can cascade into automated actions, commits, or runtime changes without verification, making downstream harm likely.
conditions: IF OpenHands uses Cursor output as the source of truth, errors can propagate into actions.
IF either agent is allowed to execute generated commands without review, cascading failures can occur.
mitigations: Require explicit verification before executing generated commands.
Have a human approve any commit or deployment step.
Compare outputs against tests before handoff.
Limit OpenHands to read-only review when consuming Cursor output.
requires-engineering: add schema validation for handoff artifacts.

E_compliance.rationale: Both profiles are docs-only and do not specify residency, certifications, or retention mismatches. Cursor handles clipboard and open files, while OpenHands handles mounted runtime files, but no compliance breach is evidenced from the profiles alone. The other agent is not separately cited because no cross-jurisdiction or certification mismatch is documented.
conditions: IF one agent is later configured for regulated data and the other is not, compliance risk may rise.
IF residency or retention policies differ across deployments, reassess the pair.
mitigations: Document data-class boundaries for each agent.
Keep regulated data out of both tools.
Review vendor retention settings before use.
Use separate tenants or environments for sensitive work.
